Concurrency

Programming with concurrency is difficult.

  • Concurrent processes/threads often need to share data or resources. If there is not some form of controlled access, a process/thread may have an inconsistent view of the data.

  • Synchronization of activities is difficult and can lead to deadlock, or starvation.

    • Deadlock: process/thread 1 cannot proceed until process/thread 2 does something, but process/thread 2 cannot proceed until process/thread 1 does something. This is a deadlock.
    • Starvation: Starvation is when one process/thread is waiting for a resource that is being held by another process/thread, but the other process/thread never releases it.

  • Debugging is maddeningly difficult because the scheduler will control the order of process/thread execution, and it is virtually impossible to recreate the same order of execution for testing purposes.

Race Condition- occurs when the result of some actions performed by a group of processes/threads depends on the order in which their execution is interleaved.

char a; //global variable, shared by all threads

void echo()
{
    cin>>a;
    cout<<a;
}

Remember that each statement in a C/C++ program gets compiled into multiple machine instructions.

For example, the statement x = x + y might be compiled into the following instructions:

mov AX, x  ;move variable values into register AX and BX
mov BX, y
add BX     ;add what is in BX to AX the 'accumulator' register
mov x, AX  ;move the result back to memory

Also remember that threads can be interrupted and removed from the running state for many different reasons such as its time slice expiring or a hardware interrupt.

This can happen at any one of the four machine instructions above.

Back to our echo example, if two threads are each using the echo() function, an unfortunate interleaving of instructions could lead to the following output:

Trying to reproduce this bug depends on the scheduler which we have no control over.

When a process/thread executes code that manipulates a shared resource (like a global variable, a file, or a database connection) we say that the process/thread is in a 'critical section' of the code.

The execution of criticial sections must be mutually exclusive (i.e. only one process/thread can be in the critical section at any given time).

Each process/thread must request permission to enter a critical section of code. It is only allowed to execute the critical section if no other process/thread is currently executing inside of it.

The critical section is the block of code that manipulates the shared resource. It must be protected by the entry and exit sections to ensure mutual exclusion.

The entry section is a block of code that is responsible for requesting permission to enter the critical section.

The exit section is a block of code that is responsible for leaving the critical section and allowing another thread to enter.

The remainder section is the block of code that does not manipulate the shared resource. It can be executed by any thread at any time without any risk of a race condition.

while(true)
{
    //request permission to enter critical section- 
    //may be permitted if no other threads are in the crit sec
    //or must wait if another threads is in the crit sec
    ENTRY SECTION

        //only one thread can be in this section at a time
        critical section

    //leaving the CS may allow another thread to enter 
    //the CS
    EXIT SECTION

    //non-critical section code, no risk of a race condition
    remainder section
}

We will have to specify entry and exit sections in order to come up with a solution to the critical section problem.

Requirements for a solution to the critical section problem:

  1. Mutual Exclusion- only one process/thread can be in the critical section at one time

  2. No deadlock or starvation.

  3. No assumptions can be made about the number of processes/threads or their relative speeds.

  4. Processes/threads remain in the critical section for a finite amount of time.

  5. Progress: if no process/thread is in the critical section a process/thread must be allowed to enter.

Progress

All code that uses a shared resource has to be checked to make sure it does not cause a deadlock or starvation.

Here are two chunks of code that could have been written by different teams that don't even know each other exists.

Process/Thread(1)           Process/Thread(2)
  1. getResource1();          1. getResource2();
  2. getResource2();          2. getResource1();
  3. ...                      3. ...
  4. releaseResource2();      4. releaseResource1();
  5. releaseResource1();      5. releaseResource2();

If process/thread 1's timeslice expires after step 1 and process/thread 2 is scheduled to run next, it will get resource 2 in step 2.

Now process/thread 1 is waiting for resource 2 and process/thread 2 is waiting for resource 1. This is a deadlock.

Starvation can occur if process/thread 1 is waiting for resource 1 and process/thread 2 is waiting for resource 2, but process/thread 3 keeps getting scheduled and it keeps getting resource 1 and resource 2 before process/thread 1 and process/thread 2 can get them.

Mutual Exclusion Approaches (SW and HW solutions)

Software Solutions to the Critical Section Problem

Pure software solution (we the programmers handle mutual exclusion ourselves).

Algorithm 1- Strict Alteration

Imagine we declared a global variable to keep track of whose turn it is to enter the critical section.

turn = i;

Thread(i)                           Thread(j)
while(true)                         while(true)
{                                   {
    //while not my turn                 //while not my turn
    while(turn != i)                    while(turn != j)
    {                                   {
        //do nothing- busy wait             //do nothing- busy wait
    }                                   }

    critical section                    critical section
    ...                                 ...

    //its your turn now                 //its your turn now
    turn = j;                           turn = i;

    remainder section                   remainder section
    ...                                 ...
}                                   }

This solution does guarantee mutual exclusion. However, it requires strict alteration of access.

Algorithm 2-

Before we had problems using the shared, global turn variable for writing. This lead to strict alteration and progress problems.

A process/thread can read the other process/thread's variable but it cannot write to it.

//            i      j
flags[2] = {false, false};

Thread(i)                           Thread(j)
while(true)                         while(true)
{                                   {
    //write to my flag                  //write to my flag 
    flags[i] = true;                    flags[j] = true;

    //read your flag                     //read your flag
    while(flags[j])                      while(flags[i])
    {                                   {
        //do nothing- busy wait             //do nothing- busy wait
    }                                   }

    critical section                    critical section
    ...                                 ...
    //done with crit sec                //done with crit sec
    flags[i] = false;                   flags[j] = false;

    remainder section                   remainder section
    ...                                 ...
}                                   }

Pop Quiz: Does this solution guarantee mutual exclusion? Does it guarantee progress? Why or why not?

Algorithm 3- Peterson's Solution

This solution is a combination of the previous two solutions.

It uses a shared variable to keep track of whose turn it is, but it also uses the flags array to indicate that a process/thread wants to enter the critical section.

flags[2] = {false, false};
turn = 0;

Thread(i)                           Thread(j)
while(true)                         while(true)
{                                   {
    //I want to use resource
    flags[i] = true;                    flags[j] = true;
    
    //I'll defer though
    turn = j;                           turn = i;

    //while the other wants to go
    while(flags[j] && turn == j)        while(flags[i] && turn == i)
    {                                   {
        //do nothing- busy wait             //do nothing- busy wait
    }                                   }

    critical section                    critical section
    ...                                 ...
    flags[i] = false;                   flags[j] = false;

    remainder section                   remainder section
    ...                                 ...
}                                   }

This solves the previous problem because only one of the threads can have set the turn variable last so this guarantees that one of the threads will defer to the other.

Drawbacks of software solutions:

  • They rely on busy wait instead of blocking, which is not a good use of the CPU. The process/thread is consuming CPU cycles while it is waiting to enter the critical section.
  • It gets more complicated as the number of processes/threads increases. We would need an array of flags and a turn variable for each pair of processes/threads. This does not scale well.

Hardware Solutions to the Critical Section Problem

Disabling Interrupts

One approach to handle the timeslice problem is to disable interrupts while a process/thread is in the critical section.

If we disable interrupts while a process/thread is in the critical section, then the scheduler will not be able to interrupt the process/thread and it will not be removed from the running state until it finishes the critical section.

Thread(i)                   Thread(j)
while(true)                 while(true)
{                           {
    disable interrupts;         disable interrupts;
        critical section            critical section
        ...                         ...
    enable interrupts;          enable interrupts;
    
    remainder section           remainder section
    ...                         ...
}                           }

However, this only works on a uniprocessor system. If there are multiple processors, disabling interrupts on one processor does not prevent another processor from executing a different thread eliminating mutual exclusion.

These days almost all computers are multiprocessor systems, so this solution is not very practical.

Performance is also a concern because we are disabling interrupts which can lead to increased latency for handling interrupts.

An I/O operation in a critical section means that we can't block it waiting for the I/O interrupt to signal it is complete.

TestAndSet Instruction

An alternative is to use a special hardware-based processor instruction.

Some processors have a special instruction called testAndSet that can carry out two actions atomically (they can't be interrupted) on the same memory location.

How Does Hardware Make This Atomic?

On a single-core system, the CPU simply disables interrupts for the duration of the instruction. No context switch can occur mid-instruction.

On a multi-core system (like the SMP architecture we discussed earlier), disabling interrupts on one core doesn't stop another core from accessing the same memory. Instead, the hardware uses one of these mechanisms:

  • Bus locking: The CPU asserts a LOCK signal on the memory bus, preventing any other core from accessing memory until the instruction completes. This is simple but can hurt performance.

  • Cache coherency protocols: Modern CPUs use protocols like MESI (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) to coordinate cache access. The core executing testAndSet gains exclusive ownership of the cache line containing the lock variable. Other cores trying to access that cache line must wait.

// This is atomic at the hardware level, not just because interrupts are disabled
bool testAndSet(int& target)
{
    //0 means that the resource is available
    //1 means that it is not available
    bool old = (target == 1);  // was it locked?
     
    target = 1; // now it's locked                                                              
    return old; // return old value
}

int lock = 0;

Thread(i)                       Thread(j)
while(true)                     while(true)
{                               {
    //no risk like before
    while(testAndSet(lock))        while(testAndSet(lock))
    {                               {
        //do nothing- busy wait         //do nothing- busy wait
    }                               }
    critical section                critical section
    ...                             ...
    ...                             ...
    lock = 0;                       lock = 0;
    remainder section               remainder section
    ...                             ...
}                               }

Mutual exclusion is preserved but it still uses busy wait and starvation may occur if one process/thread is much faster than the other.

Writing concurrent code using these low level techniques is very difficult and error prone.

Next, we'll look at some higher level synchronization primitives that can be used to make concurrent programming easier and less error prone.

Where Are These Primitives Used in the Real World?

These low-level synchronization mechanisms aren't just academic exercises. They're the foundation of concurrent systems you use every day:

Operating System Kernels

  • The Linux kernel uses spinlocks built on testAndSet-style instructions for short critical sections where sleeping would be inappropriate (e.g., interrupt handlers).
  • When you call fork() or allocate memory, the kernel uses these primitives internally to protect its data structures.

Database Systems

  • Database engines like MySQL and PostgreSQL use locks to ensure transaction isolation. When two transactions try to modify the same row, one must wait.
  • The "ACID" properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) that databases guarantee depend on these mutual exclusion techniques.

Web Servers

  • A web server handling thousands of concurrent connections must protect shared resources like connection pools, caches, and session stores.
  • The nginx web server uses spinlocks for its worker processes to coordinate access to shared memory.

Programming Language Runtimes

  • Java's synchronized keyword and Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) are built on these primitives.
  • When you use std::mutex in C++, you're using a higher-level abstraction over testAndSet or similar instructions.

Embedded Systems

  • Pacemakers, anti-lock braking systems, and flight control software use these techniques to ensure that critical operations complete without interference.
  • The consequences of race conditions in these systems can be fatal, which is why formal verification of concurrent code is common in safety-critical industries.

Understanding these primitives helps you appreciate why higher-level constructs (like semaphores, mutexes, and monitors) exist and when you might need to drop down to this level for performance reasons.

Every solution in this lecture uses busy waiting. Recall from our discussion of process states that busy waiting keeps a thread in the running state, consuming CPU cycles while it waits.

Semaphores will eliminate this by using a queue and moving threads to the blocked state instead.
